content.text: {"answer":"Low-precision arithmetic can speed up training, but it needs stability, reduced quantization error, and careful handling of communication/memory. For FP4 training, “Stable FP4 Training via Transposition-Invariant Block Quantization” shows FP4 instability can come from forward/backward scale inconsistency under tensor transposition, and proposes 2D block FP4 quantization with transposition-invariant scaling, truncation-free scaling, and stochastic rounding; it reports end-to-end FP4 training that closely matches BF16 performance on models up to 30B MoE and training up to 100B tokens [3]. “Four Over Six” improves NVFP4 by adaptively scaling blocks to reduce quantization error, reporting pre-training loss closer to BF16 than other NVFP4 recipes [2]. “What Matters for NVFP4 Training?” compares NVFP4 recipes at medium scale and proposes an optimized recipe using ingredients like unbiased gradient estimation to improve accuracy recovery [1].\n\nFor distributed settings on private or device-edge systems, the supplied results do not directly cover private devices with low-precision training across the network end-to-end. However, “AGoQ” targets distributed training efficiency by quantizing activations and gradients to reduce memory and shorten communication time, reporting training-speed improvements and convergence/accuracy comparable to prior systems [7]. “RockNet” presents distributed learning on ultra-low-power devices using wireless multi-hop protocols and reports reduced per-device memory/latency/energy when scaling from one device to 20, but it does not focus specifically on low-precision numeric formats for accelerating training [8].","grounded":true}
